chunks: Muhammad ibn Yahya, from Ahmad ibn Muhammad, from Ali ibn al-Hakam, from Rifa'ah al-Nakhhas, from a man, from Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him), who said:
Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him) comforted a man for his son, so he said: 'Allah is better for your son than you are, and the reward of Allah is better for you than your son.'
So when his sobbing reached him afterwards, he returned to him and said to him: 'The Messenger of Allah (peace be upon him and his family) has passed away, so what is for you with it is similar.'

So he said, 'My son was a drunkard.' So he (peace be upon him) said: 'In front of him are three qualities: the testimony that there is no god except Allah, and the mercy of Allah, and the intercession of the Messenger of Allah (peace be upon him and his family). So one of them will not be missed for him, if Allah wills.'

key_terms.مُرَهَّقاً: a drunkard or one who consumed intoxicants

ai.seo_question: How does the Imam comfort a father grieving over a son who was a sinner?
ai.summary: This hadith from al-Kafi illustrates the Shia doctrine of *al-‘Uqub* (consequences) and the balance between divine justice and mercy, specifically addressing the fate of those who die in a state of sin but with underlying faith. Imam al-Sadiq (peace be upon him) comforts the father by highlighting three guarantees for the deceased: the testimony of monotheism (*Shahada*), Allah’s mercy, and the Prophet’s intercession (*Shafa’ah*), ensuring that at least one of these prevents eternal punishment. This narrative underscores the Shia emphasis on the Prophet’s role as an intercessor and the reliability of divine mercy even for those with significant flaws, provided they hold the core tenets of faith.
